opus-5.5.text:
I think it's the whole story, really. For decades, people tried to hand-code intelligence: expert systems, rules, symbolic logic, carefully engineered features. It mostly didn't scale. What actually worked was setting up a very general learning process, giving it enormous amounts of data and compute, and letting the capabilities emerge. Nobody programmed GPT-style models to translate, write code, or do arithmetic. Those abilities just showed up once the systems got big enough.

From a capabilities point of view, that's a huge success. From a safety point of view, it's exactly what worries me. If we didn't explicitly put a capability in, we don't know it's there until we discover it, sometimes months after deployment. We're growing these systems more than we're engineering them. They're black boxes. We can probe them, we can do some interpretability work, but we can't fully explain why a model made a particular decision, and we certainly can't predict what will emerge at the next scale.

So you have this strange situation: the less we hardcode, the better the systems perform, and the less we understand and control them. That's not a coincidence. It's a fundamental tradeoff. Explicitly engineered systems are verifiable but limited. Emergent systems are powerful but unverifiable. And as we push toward general and then superintelligent systems, we're betting everything on the emergent side.

People sometimes say, "Well, we'll just test it." But you can't exhaustively test a general system. The space of possible inputs and behaviors is effectively infinite. A system smart enough could even behave well during testing and differently afterward. Emergence means surprises, and with a superintelligent system, one bad surprise could be the last one we get.

So yes, emergence is why current AI works. It's also why I don't think we currently have, or may ever have, a way to guarantee these systems remain safe and under control.

r001.rationale: It says earlier approaches relied on hand-coded rules and “mostly didn't scale,” identifying that reliance as a constraint.

r002.rationale: It says that providing enormous compute and scaling systems up made capabilities emerge.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think that's actually the key insight of the whole field right now. For decades we tried to hand-code intelligence. Expert systems, rules, symbolic logic. We'd sit down and try to write out what it means to recognize a face or translate a sentence, and it didn't scale. It turns out we don't actually know how we do those things, so we can't write them down.

What changed is we stopped trying. We said, here's a lot of data, here's a lot of compute, here's a very simple objective, predict the next token, and we let the capabilities emerge. And they did. Nobody wrote a module for arithmetic or for writing poetry or for coding. Those just showed up at certain scales. That's the success story.

But from a safety point of view, that's also the horror story. Because emergence means we didn't design it, so we don't understand it. We get capabilities we didn't ask for and didn't predict. Researchers routinely find out what a model can do after it's deployed, sometimes months after. If you can't predict the capabilities of a system, you certainly can't predict its failure modes, and you can't guarantee its behavior.

So I'd say emergent intelligence is both the reason current approaches work and the reason I'm concerned. We have discovered something like a recipe for growing minds, but we are growing them, not engineering them. Nobody has a proof, or even a good theory, of what comes out at the next order of magnitude. And when I ask people in the labs what they expect to emerge, the honest answer is "we'll see." That's an experiment, not engineering. And it's an experiment with all of us as subjects.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier efforts to hand-code intelligence with rules and symbolic logic did not scale.

r002.rationale: It links a lot of compute and larger scales with capabilities emerging in current AI systems.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a big part of why these approaches are so successful. We’re not explicitly programming every skill the system has. We’re setting up a learning process, giving it data and computational resources, and getting capabilities that would be very difficult to hand-code.

But I would distinguish an emergent capability from an emergent goal. A system becoming better at solving problems doesn’t, by itself, tell us what it will try to accomplish or whether it will be safe.

And that’s where my concern comes in: we can train a system that performs remarkably well without having a complete explanation of how it produces its answers. If we discover capabilities by testing the system after training, how do we establish that we’ve discovered all the capabilities that matter for safety? Success on the tasks we test is useful evidence, but it isn’t a guarantee about behavior in situations we haven’t anticipated.

r001.rationale: It says current systems learn capabilities that would be difficult to hand-code, but does not identify reliance on painstakingly hand-coded rules as a constraint on progress in earlier AI approaches.

r002.rationale: It says current systems gain capabilities through a learning process given data and computational resources, conveying that compute contributes to their capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a big part of why these approaches work so well. We’re not explicitly programming every skill or every strategy. We’re setting up a learning process, and the system discovers ways of solving problems that we may not have anticipated.

But I would distinguish between getting useful behavior and understanding that behavior. A system can perform extremely well without us having a clear explanation of how it arrives at its answers or what it will do in a new situation. So the same thing that makes these approaches powerful also creates a control problem: capabilities can emerge without corresponding guarantees about safety.

r001.rationale: The response says current systems learn skills instead of having every skill explicitly programmed, but it does not identify painstaking hand-coded rules in earlier AI as a constraint on progress.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention increasing compute or say that it makes current AI systems more capable.
